turns: A rectangle is 3 m by 4 m. What is its area?
Give that in square feet.
replies: 12 m² 📐

129.17 ft² 📐 To get from square meters to square feet, we use the conversion factor for length and apply it twice because area is two-dimensional. One meter equals approximately 3.28084 feet. Since a rectangle’s area is width times height, we multiply those converted dimensions together: $1 \text{ m}^2 = (3.28084 \text{ ft}) \times (3.28084 \text{ ft})$, which gives us roughly 10.7639 square feet per square meter.

For your specific rectangle, the area is $3 \text{ m} \times 4 \text{ m}$, or 12 square meters total. When we convert that to imperial units, it’s simply $12 \times 10.7639$, which lands us at approximately 129.17 square feet 📐 The reason we multiply by roughly 10.76 is that area scales with the square of length, so a small change in linear units becomes much larger when squared. Think about it this way: if one meter were exactly three feet (a nice round number for illustration), then an area of one square meter would be $3 \text{ ft} \times 3 \text{ ft}$, which equals nine square feet. In reality, a single meter is actually closer to 3.28084 feet long. When you multiply that length by itself—$3.28084 \times 3.28084$—you get approximately $10.7639$. This means every square meter on your floor plan covers about ten and three-quarters of a square foot in the imperial system 📐

To see how this works for any shape, just take its area in meters squared and multiply it by that conversion factor we discussed earlier. For example, if you had a small rug measuring 2 m², you would simply calculate $2 \times 10.7639$, which gives you about 21.5 square feet 📐 It is always much easier to convert the total area at once rather than converting each side individually and then multiplying them out again, though both methods will lead you to the same final number for your rectangle!

turns: Give me a prime number strictly between 24 and 28.
replies:
There isn't one. The whole numbers strictly between 24 and 28 are 25, 26, and 27 — none of them are prime 🚫.

To see why there’s nothing in that gap, let’s look at each number between 24 and 28 one by one. A prime is a whole number greater than 1 that has exactly two factors: 1 and itself.

First up is 25. It looks like it might be prime because it ends in 5 (and we often think of numbers ending in odd digits as potentially prime), but if you try dividing it by anything, you’ll find $5 \times 5 = 25$. Since it has a factor other than itself and one, it’s composite.

Next is 26. This is an even number greater than 2, so we know right away it can be divided by 2 ($13 \times 2$). That immediately knocks it out of the prime club because primes (except for 2) must be odd to avoid being divisible by two.

Finally, there’s 27. It feels like a "prime-ish" number because it doesn’t end in an even digit or five, but if you add its digits ($2 + 7 = 9$), that tells us it’s divisible by 3. And indeed, $3 \times 9 = 27$.

So we have three numbers: one is a square of a prime (5²), one is even (divisible by 2), and one is a multiple of 3 ($3^3$). They are all composite. The next prime after 24 isn’t until you reach 29, which sits just outside your requested range 🛑.
